anomaly_def.Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly : Static mismatch between the physical data model (tables, partitions, indexes, data types, constraints) and the workload’s access patterns, forcing otherwise well-written SQL into inherently inefficient access paths.
Query Plan Selection Anomaly : Optimizer chooses a sub-optimal plan despite accurate statistics, often because of cost-model quirks, parameter sniffing, or unstable plan-cache behavior, leading to erratic or inefficient execution strategies.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly : Underlying storage subsystem cannot deliver the read/write throughput, IOPS, or latency required by the workload, so physical I/O waits dominate even when the engine submits requests correctly.

When these three root causes coexist, the database exhibits compound symptoms: frequent full-table scans or non-covering index lookups (from the design flaw) are paired with erratic plan flips to the least efficient strategies (from optimizer mis-selection), dramatically inflating the volume of physical I/O pushed onto an already saturated storage layer. The result is runaway buffer-cache churn, persistently deep I/O queues, alternating CPU and I/O stalls, unpredictable response-time spikes, and batch or ETL jobs that oscillate between slow and extremely slow depending on which bad plan is chosen. Monitoring tools show a mixture of high logical reads, excessive physical reads, plan instability warnings, and storage wait events, making it difficult to attribute slowness to a single layer.

Causal chain: Poor schema and index design increases the baseline data touched per statement; sub-optimal plan selection further magnifies that footprint by discarding whatever limited selectivity the existing indexes could provide. The inflated I/O demand collides with a storage subsystem that is already throughput-bound, so physical read/write latencies rise sharply, feeding back into the optimizer’s runtime feedback or adaptive mechanisms and sometimes triggering even worse re-optimization or plan eviction. Conversely, storage congestion slows the collection of execution feedback and prolongs compile times, increasing the window in which stale or wrong plans are reused. Together, the three anomalies reinforce each other, amplifying workload pressure, obscuring diagnosis, and creating a vicious cycle of design inefficiency, plan instability, and I/O saturation.

entry.official_description: Check constraint '%-.192s' refers to non-existing column '%-.192s'.
entry.cause_analysis: The failure is typically associated with logical data inconsistency, structural corruption, uniqueness conflicts, or referential-integrity rules being violated by the workload or storage state.
entry.solution_guidance: Validate data consistency, inspect constraints and index integrity, and check whether data-cleaning, repair, or workload correction is required before retrying.
